items.title: British women got the vote in two instalments: 1918 and 1928
items.claim: When did UK women win equal voting rights with men?

options.text: 1918 — full equal franchise immediately after WWI
1918 gave the vote to women over 30 meeting property qualifications (around 8.4 million); 1928 (Equal Franchise Act) gave it to all women over 21 on the same terms as men

items.reveal:
The Representation of the People Act 1918 enfranchised women over 30 who were householders, married to householders, occupiers of property at £5+ rent or university graduates. Men got the vote at 21 (or 19 if a serviceman).

The WSPU (Pankhursts, 1903), the NUWSS (Millicent Fawcett, constitutionalist) and women's war work all contributed. The 1918 compromise was partly designed to keep women a minority of the electorate.

The Equal Franchise Act 1928 gave women the vote at 21 on the same terms as men. Emmeline Pankhurst died on 14 June 1928, weeks before it took effect.
items.why: Reform is rarely complete in one step. The 10-year gap between 1918 and 1928 is itself part of the history — a partial victory deliberately designed to limit female political weight.

items.title: Cromwell did not set out to be a republican
items.claim: What were Oliver Cromwell's politics in 1642?

options.text: He had been a republican agitator since the 1620s
He was a Huntingdonshire MP and country gentleman who fought for Parliament against the king's policies but moved towards regicide only by late 1648
He was a paid Dutch agent from the start
He was a Leveller from the outset

items.reveal:
Cromwell entered the 1640 Long Parliament as MP for Cambridge. As late as 1647 he was negotiating with Charles I (the Heads of the Proposals). The king's plotting with the Scots — the Second Civil War of 1648 — convinced Cromwell that Charles could not be trusted.

Pride's Purge (December 1648) removed MPs likely to negotiate. The Rump Parliament tried and executed the king on 30 January 1649. Cromwell signed the death warrant but had not been pushing for it years earlier.

He later dissolved the Rump (1653) and accepted the title Lord Protector, refusing the crown in 1657.
items.why: The 'inevitable republican' Cromwell of memory is partly constructed by 19th-century liberals (Macaulay, Carlyle). The actual man's politics shifted under pressure of events.

items.title: The Domesday Book recorded almost every pig in England
items.claim: William I commissioned the Domesday survey in 1085, completed 1086. How detailed was it?

options.text: It listed only the major landholders and royal manors
It recorded landholders, ploughs, mills, fishponds, livestock and even individual peasants down to the level of swineherds — over 13,000 places
It was a list of military obligations only

items.reveal_title: Not one ox or cow escaped
items.reveal:
The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (E text) complained: 'So very narrowly did he have it investigated that there was no single hide nor a yard of land, nor indeed (it is a shame to relate but it seemed no shame to him to do) one ox nor one cow nor one pig which was left out.'

Commissioners visited every shire, took sworn testimony, and produced the survey in around a year. The original manuscripts (Great Domesday and Little Domesday) survive at The National Archives, Kew.
items.why: Medieval government is often dismissed as primitive. Domesday is more administratively detailed than anything attempted in Europe for centuries afterwards.
